payload.subject: Introducing async handler dispatch (`go p.handleRequest`) while simultaneously reversing shutdown order (close-conn-first instead of drain-pump-first) broke `TestMalformedJSON` with EOF. The test expected an error response but the conn was closed before the write pump could flush it. The correct order is: signal pump to stop → wait for pump to drain → then call shutdown, because in all realistic exit paths the pump is safe to drain before closing (EOF already closed, decode-error remote still reading, ctx-cancel conn already closed by watcher).

FAIL
FAIL	github.com/mistakenot/auto-shared/rpc	0.680s
The async handler dispatch changed timing — the error response may be enqueued but the peer shuts down before the pump can write it.

The peer shutdown sequence (drain → close conn → fail waiters) has a subtle ordering tension: draining before closing lets error responses reach the remote, but closing first prevents pump deadlocks on stalled connections.

payload.suggested_generalization: When adding async handler dispatch to a read-loop/write-pump peer, keep shutdown order as drain-first (signal pump stop → wait for pump → then close conn); closing the conn first drops in-flight error responses and breaks tests that assert on error frames.

payload.subject: A unit-tested primitive interface with fake resolvers gives no signal about whether the real caller actually passes an implementation — the production call path can silently use nil/zero, bypassing the feature entirely.

payload.subject: When resource A (e.g. a canonical URL) is needed to open resource B (e.g. a cache repo), and B's live state is needed to complete A's work (e.g. ref resolution), the solution is a two-phase approach: run A cheaply once to get enough output to open B, then re-run A with B available to complete the full computation.

payload.context: Deep-link ref splitting needs a live ref set only available after the cache clone, but the cache open call needs the canonical URL that only ParseSource produces. Solved by parsing twice: once (no resolver) to get the URL, open the cache, then re-parse with a cache-backed resolver.
payload.suggested_generalization: When initialization has a circular dependency (A needs B's output, B needs A's output), use a two-phase approach: run A cheaply to seed B, then re-run A with B fully available; document the ordering constraint explicitly in code comments.

payload.subject: A security gate CLI flag was silently a no-op because the gate function was called with nil for the parameter the flag was supposed to populate; the fix must narrow-scope the value to the project's explicit opt-in list rather than blanket-approving all callers, to avoid widening the trust surface.

payload.subject: Parallel context-gathering subagents dispatched at the start of a planning phase may complete after the coordinator has already moved on. payload.use_when: writing Go code that creates or persists config files containing credentials, tokens, or secret keys
payload.content: Never write credential or API-key config files through shared WriteJSONFile helpers that unconditionally apply mode 0644. Implement a dedicated WriteSecure function that: creates the parent directory at 0700, writes the file, then calls os.Chmod(path, 0600). Enforce the resulting file-mode bits with a unit test that stats the file after writing.
payload.causal_note: Shared JSON helpers create world-readable 0644 files; any config storing an API key or access key is then readable by all local users, violating least-privilege. The bug is invisible at runtime.

payload.use_when: implementing AWS S3 uploads or hand-rolling SigV4 request signing in Go
payload.content: When hand-rolling AWS SigV4 in Go, apply two invariants: (1) set url.URL.RawPath to the AWS uriEncode output before building the request so that EscapedPath() returns the exact bytes the signer hashes — Go's default escaping diverges from uriEncode for +, :, and space, causing silent signature failures; (2) never source upload data from a pipe or /dev/stdin because os.Stat() returns size 0, breaking the mandatory Content-Length header — materialize the source to a named temp file first.
payload.causal_note: Both failure modes produce the same symptom (AWS rejects the request) but are invisible locally: URL-escaping mismatches only surface for keys with special characters; piped stdin stats to zero size which silently breaks SigV4 PUT.

payload.use_when: refactoring Cobra init()-based commands into NewXxxCmd() constructors, or adding boolean CLI flags to commands with expected default-on behaviors
payload.content: When extracting Cobra init() registrations into a NewXxxCmd() constructor, every sub-constructor (newRunCmd, newServeCmd, etc.) must allocate a fresh cobra.Command value internally — never mutate a package-level *cobra.Command variable — so that calling the constructor twice (as test harnesses do) does not panic with 'flag redefined'. Separately, after drafting any boolean flag, audit its Default value against the acceptance criteria: a `false` default silently voids a 'default-enabled' AC with no compile or test failure.
payload.causal_note: Package-level cobra.Command + re-registration panics on the second call, which integration tests trigger by building the command tree per test case. False boolean defaults silently create no-op production installs when the AC requires the behavior to be on by default. Both failure modes are invisible to the compiler.

payload.use_when: writing E2E or integration tests that invoke a Go CLI binary via exec.Command and parse structured (JSON) output, or that start a Go HTTP server on a dynamic port
payload.content: In E2E CLI tests, apply two patterns: (1) never use exec.Command with CombinedOutput() when parsing JSON stdout — always attach separate Stdout and Stderr pipe captures so that any diagnostic stderr output cannot silently corrupt the JSON stream (a class of bug that Cobra unit tests using cmd.SetOut/SetErr will never catch); (2) for server-under-test startup, use net.Listen("tcp", addr) + srv.Serve(ln) and write the real bound address from ln.Addr() to a --ready-file; never rely on scraping a stderr banner, which is racy.
payload.causal_note: CombinedOutput() mixes stderr into stdout; adding any diagnostic line later silently breaks JSON parsing in existing tests. Banner-scraping races with the listener being ready; the ready-file pattern is deterministic.

payload.use_when: writing a long-running Go server, daemon, or watch command using Cobra
payload.content: Wire signal.NotifyContext(cmd.Context(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM) inside the individual serve/watch Cobra command's RunE function, not in main.go. main.go passes context.Background() which never cancels, making any signal handling placed there dead code. Always pass a context.WithTimeout deadline to srv.Shutdown() to prevent it from blocking indefinitely.
payload.causal_note: Signal handling in main.go is silently unreachable because Cobra receives a non-cancellable Background context; the server must be force-killed rather than shutting down cleanly. The bug produces no compile or test failure.

payload.use_when: Adding a new lifecycle value, kind, or tag to a shared valid-set in Go, or writing a new command that calls a shared validate() function
payload.content: Put all cross-field invariants (e.g., field A present implies field B must be set; new lifecycle member implies provenance path is required) in the shared validate() function, not in per-command handlers. After adding a member to any shared valid-set, immediately trace every command that now reaches that member through the shared enum check, and introduce the matching guard in validate() rather than in the individual command.
payload.causal_note: Per-command guards are bypassed by every other command entry point: an enforced lifecycle invariant placed only in the graduate handler was silently skipped by create and edit (ob-83282db2). Adding 'enforced' to validLifecycles then let create/edit bypass the provenance gate entirely (ob-e1607e80).

payload.use_when: Writing or reviewing a content-hash ID minting function in Go, especially for idempotent event-sourced or projection-based storage
payload.content: Never make a content-hash ID minting function fully variadic. Require at least one content argument via a non-variadic first parameter (e.g., NewRuleID(first string, rest ...string)) or return an error/panic on empty input. A parts ...string signature compiles cleanly with zero args, mints a constant collision hash, and silently drops all-but-first events in any idempotency-by-ID-projection design — causing data loss with no compile error and no test failure.
payload.causal_note: Zero-arg calls to NewRuleID compiled cleanly and minted the same constant ID for every missed caller; the projection then dropped all subsequent events as duplicates, silently losing data (ob-8e2befa1).

payload.use_when: Writing a Go test that asserts on a field populated from env-var detection (session IDs, host IDs) and serialized with omitempty
payload.content: Explicitly set every env var inside any test that asserts on a field populated from env-var detection (e.g., events.DetectSessionID()) and serialized with omitempty. Never rely on the ambient dev-shell environment. A clean CI runner will omit the field entirely, making the test pass locally while silently failing on CI — the test is checking the host environment, not the code.
payload.causal_note: TestE2ELoopQuickstart asserted session_id appeared in gap rows; session_id is omitempty and resolves from env vars absent on CI, so the test passed locally and failed on clean runners (ob-57f70162).

payload.use_when: Filtering session or event records by 'current repository' in code that runs inside a worktree-based development workflow
payload.content: Scope session and event records to the current repository by normalized git remote, not by workspace or cwd filesystem path. In a worktree workflow, each worktree has a distinct absolute path for the same repo; path-equality scoping fragments one repo's records into disjoint sets and silently misses the majority.
payload.causal_note: Scoping by Workspace path would have split one repo's session queue into several disjoint queues — one per active worktree — effectively losing most of the repo's mined sessions (ob-5fd32408). A related normalization bug (ob-f245ee59) also arose from inconsistent remote URL treatment across code paths.

payload.use_when: Designing or extending an event-sourced Go package where consumer packages import a shared events package
payload.content: In event-sourced Go packages, define ALL payload sub-types — status enums, nested structs, domain value types — inside the events package itself, never in consumer packages. The dependency arrow must flow one way: consumers import events, events imports nothing from consumers. Any payload type placed in a consumer package that the events package also needs creates a compile-blocking import cycle.
payload.causal_note: Placing Signals in the miner consumer package while events imported miner for AppendEvent and AckStatus created a compile-blocking cycle that required moving all payload sub-types back into the events package (ob-72d7ed43).

payload.use_when: writing or debugging pre-commit hooks or Makefile recipes that invoke git-aware tools, when working in or dispatching to a linked git worktree
payload.content: In pre-commit hooks and Makefile recipes called by them, explicitly unset GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, and GIT_INDEX_FILE before calling any git-aware tool (e.g., `env -u GIT_DIR -u GIT_WORK_TREE -u GIT_INDEX_FILE make pre-commit`); in linked worktrees git injects these vars into hook execution and any subprocess inheriting them targets the wrong repository root.
payload.causal_note: Git injects GIT_DIR/GIT_WORK_TREE/GIT_INDEX_FILE into hook processes in linked worktrees. ob-7ae7dd35: Makefile recipes inside pre-commit failed with confusing errors unrelated to the staged code. ob-2c59874d: `auto skill sync --check` resolved `repo:""` and reported 165 false 'incomplete cache' errors, blocking every commit in the worktree — while the exact same command ran clean outside the hook.

payload.use_when: a pre-commit lint hook fails with 'no such file or directory', 'parallel golangci-lint is running', or a machine-wide lock error while multiple worktrees are active
payload.content: When a golangci-lint pre-commit failure shows 'no such file or directory' (stale cross-worktree cache), run `golangci-lint cache clean` and retry; when it shows a lock-contention error (concurrent worktrees racing on /tmp/golangci-lint.lock), stash the change and wait for the concurrent lint load to drop before retrying — never bypass with --no-verify, as neither failure reflects a real code defect.
payload.causal_note: golangci-lint shares a cache and a machine-wide lock across all worktrees. ob-3234e7a5: a stale cache held references to files only present in a sibling worktree, producing 'no such file or directory' errors on valid code. ob-e377f2b5: 15 concurrent worktrees serialized on the global lock, causing a status-flip commit to lose the race entirely and leaving stray uncommitted edits.

payload.use_when: dispatching multiple subagents to implement phases of a task, or considering running parallel phases in the same git worktree
payload.content: Never dispatch concurrent subagents into the same git worktree: pre-commit hooks that run formatters over all source files (e.g., goimports) auto-stage untracked work from parallel phases into the wrong commit; concurrent tool runs (e.g., `npx skills install`) silently overwrite committed-correct generated files. Dispatch phases serially, and before staging generated files (e.g., `.agents/skills/`, `skills-lock.json`) diff them against HEAD to detect regressions introduced by concurrent processes.
payload.causal_note: ob-9e3f0904: concurrent Phase 1 and Phase 2 subagents in the same worktree caused goimports (run by the pre-commit hook over all files) to auto-stage Phase 2's untracked files into Phase 1's commit, corrupting attribution. ob-f91feec1: a concurrent `npx skills install` silently reverted a committed fix (`auto search` → `autosearch`) with stale generated content; the pre-commit stale-ref guard was the only safety net and the agent nearly committed the regression.

payload.use_when: writing a shell hook that calls a CLI subcommand, extending an existing hook command to emit output, or designing hooks that fire across multiple agent platforms (Claude, Codex)
payload.content: Before wiring a hook to a CLI subcommand: (1) grep the command's `Flags()` registrations to confirm each flag used in the hook stanza exists on that exact subcommand — do not assume a flag is present because a sibling command has it; (2) check whether the hook command has an established no-stdout invariant and scope any new output strictly to the event types that support responses, adding an AC that all other installed events remain silent; (3) for cross-agent hooks, verify each agent's PostToolUse trigger semantics from upstream docs rather than assuming a shared schema — Claude splits success/failure into PostToolUse vs PostToolUseFailure, while Codex fires PostToolUse on all completions with a different payload shape.
payload.causal_note: ob-57feb89d: hook stanzas called `auto skill sync --check --format json` but `sync` registered no `--format` flag (only `--text`), producing silent no-ops or pre-commit crashes caught only by Codex review, not by stub-based tests. ob-2c8319fb: Task 020 required `auto hooks fire` to be a pure observer (exit 0, no stdout); adding hookSpecificOutput JSON would break Codex Stop/SubagentStop events that reject non-empty stdout. ob-0cf2f402: a design assumed a uniform `is_error` field on PostToolUse payloads — upstream docs show the field does not exist on Claude PostToolUse and has a different shape on Codex.

payload.use_when: Writing code that reads a git remote URL from a project registry, config file, or git output and then broadcasts, logs, or transmits it to any external consumer (bus events, UI clients, network envelopes)
payload.content: Always call NormalizeRemoteURL() to strip embedded credentials (https://token:@...) from any git remote URL before it enters a bus event, log, network envelope, or stored registry entry; add a unit test asserting the emitted remote contains no '@' or credential substring.
payload.causal_note: Raw git remote URLs frequently embed live PATs (e.g. https://x-access-token:github_pat_11AB35...@github.com/...). Broadcasting the raw URL on an event bus or writing it to a log leaks those credentials to every connected client and log consumer.

payload.use_when: Processing a hook payload JSON object that includes a cwd field alongside relative file paths or tool paths
payload.content: Always resolve relative tool paths and run git operations (RepoRoot, Provenance) against the payload's cwd field, not the hook process's working directory — pass cwd explicitly to every git call, never default to os.Getwd().
payload.causal_note: The hook process cwd and the payload cwd can differ silently (e.g. the hook binary is invoked from a different directory), causing rel to be computed against the wrong root so that downstream path matchers like docs/** miss all events.

payload.use_when: Implementing a CLI command that reads, patches, or merges into a JSON config file whose schema is owned by a third party (e.g. .claude/settings.json, .codex/hooks.json, agent tool configs)
payload.content: Parse and manipulate the entire JSON document as map[string]any; never unmarshal into typed Go structs. Re-marshal the generic tree so that schema-unknown fields (timeout, args, if, commandWindows, etc.) round-trip byte-for-byte untouched.
payload.causal_note: Unmarshaling into typed structs silently drops every field not modeled in the struct on re-marshal, corrupting existing hook handler configurations and breaking unrelated agent features with no error or warning.

payload.use_when: Implementing a command that installs hooks across multiple or all agent hook events at once (mass-install, --all-events, or similar)
payload.content: Define and enforce an explicit telemetry-safe allowlist of hook events; exclude every active-control event (e.g. Claude's WorktreeCreate) where the hook's stdout is consumed as data by the agent rather than discarded — a silent exit-0 hook on those events breaks the feature without any error message.
payload.causal_note: Some hook events gate or replace agent behavior using hook stdout (WorktreeCreate must print the new worktree path). A fire-and-forget telemetry hook installed there produces no output and silently disables the feature.

payload.use_when: Implementing or testing a git hook installer, or writing E2E verification for any CLI command that installs hooks or wires bare command strings into agent configs
payload.content: Apply three checks: (a) Use git rev-parse --git-common-dir (not --git-dir) to locate the shared hooks directory — --git-dir returns a per-worktree path in linked worktrees. (b) Before dogfooding any installer that creates directories under a dot-path (.codex, .claude), verify those paths are not stray files in the repo with ls -la. (c) When verifying an installed bare command string, invoke it via sh -c '<command>' after setting PATH — calling ./bin/<binary> directly passes even when the bare installed string would fail due to PATH not including the binary.
payload.causal_note: Three independent installer failures share the same pattern of untested real-world resolution: --git-dir installs hooks in the wrong directory for linked worktrees; a stray 0-byte committed file at an expected directory path produces 'not a directory' errors that look like installer bugs; and invoking the binary by local path rather than the installed command string masks PATH resolution failures entirely.

payload.use_when: Writing or modifying Go source files inside a subagent workflow, or writing any test code that calls json.Marshal on an interface{}/any-typed value
payload.content: After writing or modifying any Go file in a subagent workflow, explicitly run gofmt -w <file> before staging — never rely on the pre-commit hook firing, since subagent file-write operations bypass git hooks entirely. Additionally always check and handle the error return of json.Marshal even in test files; the errchkjson pre-commit linter blocks commits when any-typed marshal errors are ignored.
payload.causal_note: Subagent file-write operations do not trigger git hooks, so gofmt and errchkjson linting never run automatically during the session; CI format checks and the pre-commit hook then fail on the first push, blocking the commit and requiring a fixup.

payload.use_when: preparing context.md for multi-phase subagent dispatch on any task that touches existing Go code
payload.content: In context.md, enumerate every code site the plan touches with exact file path and line range; for patterns to mirror, name the specific existing function (with file:line) rather than describing the pattern abstractly; for shared utilities used by multiple callers, list every call-site so executors see the full multi-caller picture before they start writing.
payload.causal_note: Without file:line anchors, each dispatched subagent spends its first tokens re-discovering the codebase instead of writing code. Naming abstract patterns instead of concrete functions leads to reinvention of already-solved logic (e.g. bounded-buffer write-pump). Omitting multi-caller context hides that a change will affect more sites than the one the executor is focused on.

payload.use_when: reversing a design default in a planning document, or writing context.md that describes how to implement a decision already accepted in plan.html
payload.content: After reversing a design default, grep the entire planning doc for the old framing — including Out-of-scope, Known-gaps, and Plan-steps sections — and update every occurrence before requesting review. When writing context.md implementation guidance, derive it exclusively from the accepted decision in plan.html; never edit context.md in isolation.
payload.causal_note: Old framing survives in overlooked sections and misleads reviewers into thinking the decision is still unsettled. A context.md that diverges from plan.html's accepted decision silently sends executors in the wrong direction with no error signal.

payload.use_when: transitioning from solution design to implementation planning, or scripting CLI flags into a plan or quickstart doc
payload.content: Before running /new-plan: (1) request a structured inline review of solution.md to catch architectural flaws while the phase breakdown is still fluid; (2) verify every CLI flag and subcommand the plan will script by running `<tool> --help`; (3) run a multi-persona user simulation against the draft CLI surface to surface missing contract cases (empty states, error vocabulary, snapshot persistence, read-only escapes) that review threads typically miss.
payload.causal_note: Design defects caught after the plan is written force re-architecture of already-committed phases. CLI surfaces that do not exist cause silent divergence when executors adapt without updating the doc. Missing CLI contract cases discovered post-implementation require breaking changes to an already-shipped interface.

payload.use_when: designing any link-tracking, freshness-checking, content-addressability, or bookkeeping feature that would annotate source or documentation files with computed hashes or state
payload.content: Externalize all bookkeeping hashes and mutable state to an append-only sidecar file (e.g. a JSONL event log); never embed them inline in source or documentation files.
payload.causal_note: Inline hash rewrites force every regeneration pass to touch files that have not logically changed. In one incident, 165 of 168 changed files were pure mechanical hash rewrites, making the one real authored change invisible and corrupting co-change analytics by creating false coupling signals between unrelated files.

payload.use_when: writing or reviewing task context docs for a multi-phase or subagent-delegated task
payload.content: Task context docs must include: (1) verified line-number references to every key code site (not just file paths), (2) an explicit 'gotchas' section listing known wrong patterns alongside their correct alternatives, and (3) non-obvious function-level fallback/default behaviors near integration points (e.g., 'isRuntimeImport returns true when no import_kinds set — line 432'). These specifics reduce subagent re-exploration more than high-level structural descriptions.
payload.causal_note: Without pinned line refs and explicit gotchas, subagents re-discover the same pitfalls each phase (ob-43340179: wrong subcommand names, positional signature risks). Without documented fallback behaviors, silent misclassification bugs go undetected because they are invisible to automated tests (ob-d207f7fd: lenient default triggered incorrect classifications).

payload.use_when: writing rapid.StateMachine or property-based tests that create a fresh isolated environment (t.TempDir, local git repo) per generated sequence
payload.content: Use local file:// git fixture repos (e.g. newFixture(t)) for any state that resets per sequence; never reference a remote upstream inside StateMachine.Init. When the first generated sequence fails, verify the model's expected behavior against documented SUT behavior before treating the failure as a production bug — the model itself may encode incorrect assumptions about scope or side-effects.
payload.causal_note: Each rapid.StateMachine sequence gets its own t.TempDir, resetting the cache; 100 sequences become 100 cold clones of a remote, making the suite slow, flaky offline, and rate-limit-sensitive. Additionally, the first state machine failure on a new suite is as likely to be a model bug (wrong expectation encoded) as a SUT bug, causing wasted investigation.

payload.use_when: writing a Go test that must detect a bug before a fix and still pass after it, especially when the fix alters internal function signatures
payload.content: Restrict the test to the exported public API and on-disk filesystem observations only; never call unexported functions or depend on internal signatures that the fix may rename or change. The test must compile identically against both buggy and fixed code.
payload.causal_note: A fix that renames or re-signs an internal function (e.g. planPrune) causes compilation failure for any test that called it directly, breaking the build between the 'bug detected' and 'bug fixed' states and defeating the purpose of the regression test.

payload.use_when: adding async handler dispatch (goroutine per request) to a Go read-loop / write-pump server peer
payload.content: Preserve drain-first shutdown order: signal the write pump to stop, wait for it to drain, then close the connection. Never close the connection before the pump has flushed — closing first drops any in-flight error responses before they reach the wire.
payload.causal_note: Reversing shutdown order to close-conn-first while simultaneously adding async handlers broke TestMalformedJSON with EOF: the connection was torn down before the write pump could flush the error response, causing the client to receive EOF instead of the expected error frame.

payload.use_when: implementing a Go constructor or handler that reads from disk at call time — config files, ~/.auto/*, projects.json, or any host-local state
payload.content: Inject config-loading as a functional option (e.g. WithRegistryProvider(func() Config)) with an empty/zero-value default. Never call disk-reading functions inside constructors; the default zero config must keep existing unit tests hermetic without any changes to test code.
payload.causal_note: Loading real ~/.auto/projects.json inside a constructor couples every unit test to host state, causing silent non-hermeticity: tests pass locally but fail in CI where that file is absent or contains different data.

payload.use_when: declaring a Go implementation phase done, writing per-phase verification steps, or configuring CI job commands for a Go module
payload.content: Run `make check` (or `golangci-lint run ./...`) in every per-phase verify step — `go build`, `go vet`, and `go test` are necessary but not sufficient; linters such as `modernize`, `gosec`, and `nilerr` surface real defects that standard tooling skips. Never declare a phase done without a passing full lint gate.
payload.causal_note: Omitting golangci-lint from intermediate phase gates lets lint debt accumulate silently and then block the final gate with a large batch of findings — 27 golangci-lint findings batched into Phase 4 in ob-927fd7f8, and a real `modernize` finding missed entirely by go vet/test in ob-cd123021.

payload.use_when: merging a PR from inside a task worktree, or completing any task that uses git linked worktrees where the primary checkout holds main
payload.content: From inside a task worktree, use `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{N}/merge -f merge_method=squash` instead of `gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch`; if the remote branch still needs deletion, run `git push origin --delete <branch>` separately after confirming the merge via `gh pr view --json state,mergedAt`.
payload.causal_note: `gh pr merge` tries to check out `main` locally to perform the merge and branch deletion — this always fails with "fatal: 'main' is already used by worktree" when the primary checkout holds that branch, as seen in both ob-26526206 (high severity) and ob-c64aa18c.

payload.use_when: adding a new Go module to the auto-stack monorepo, expanding the Makefile PROJECTS list, or auditing which modules are covered by aggregate CI gates
payload.content: When introducing a new module, add it to every aggregate Makefile target (test, vet, lint, race) in the same PR it is created. When widening PROJECTS to include a previously-excluded module, run lint/vet/test locally on that module first and fix all findings before the PR that widens the scope; do not ship the PROJECTS change until the module is clean.
payload.causal_note: A module absent from PROJECTS is silently excluded from all CI quality checks — the most critical shared concurrency module had never been tested in CI in ob-dba3a3d4. Adding a previously-excluded module later converts all accumulated technical debt into immediate CI blockers, as happened in ob-9495a21d.

payload.use_when: creating test fixtures under a testdata/ directory, adding Go integration test data files, or setting up any fixture files for automated tests
payload.content: After creating any file under a `testdata/` directory, immediately run `git check-ignore -v <path>` to confirm it is not excluded. If it is, add an explicit `!<module>/testdata/` un-ignore entry to `.gitignore` before committing any test that depends on those fixtures.
payload.causal_note: The repo's default `**/testdata/` gitignore rule causes `git add` to silently stage nothing with no error message — fixtures exist locally (local tests pass) but are never committed, producing CI failures with 'no such file or directory' on every clean checkout.

payload.use_when: creating an execution worktree, dispatching a subagent phase, or branching a feature from main in a Go workspace
payload.content: Before creating any execution worktree or dispatching a subagent phase, verify the committed tree compiles by running `go build ./...` from a fresh checkout of `origin/main` — not from the primary working directory — to ensure no untracked files are silently satisfying references in committed code.
payload.causal_note: Untracked source files in the primary checkout can satisfy imports and symbol references that exist in committed code, masking compiler errors. Every worktree branched from the committed tree fails to compile while the primary checkout with the untracked file builds fine, as in ob-02659b89 (high severity).

payload.use_when: dispatching subagents to write files in a shared git worktree, or verifying that a subagent phase completed successfully
payload.content: Dispatch file-writing subagents serially, never concurrently, in a shared worktree. After each subagent reports completion, independently verify the expected files exist on disk (`git status`, `test -f`, `grep`) before the next agent starts or the step is marked done. When a subagent is killed mid-run, inspect the worktree for partial output first — if files were written, complete the phase from the coordinator rather than re-dispatching the same prompt. Never accept an agent's self-reported success as ground truth: silent write loss and hallucinated 'already done' are both real failure modes.
payload.causal_note: Concurrent subagents sharing a worktree silently dropped ~7 out of 9 packages' Phase 2 edits with no error output (ob-0b5ff9c0). In the same session an agent claimed files were complete when git showed them unmodified (ob-019819f1). A separate session found that re-dispatching a killed subagent without inspecting the worktree wasted two retries — the files were already half-written (ob-bcb9949a). All three failure modes are eliminated by serial dispatch + on-disk verification.

payload.use_when: running or debugging lint failures in a Go worktree, especially when errors reference file paths that look unfamiliar or from other branches
payload.content: Use `golangci-lint run` (not just `go vet`) as the post-phase lint gate — it catches `ineffassign` and other issues that `go vet` silently ignores. If golangci-lint reports errors referencing file paths outside the current worktree (e.g., paths matching a deleted sibling task worktree), run `golangci-lint cache clean` before treating any failure as real; the shared on-disk cache retains stale analysis entries for paths that no longer exist.
payload.causal_note: A deleted sibling worktree's paths remained in the shared golangci-lint cache, causing a clean branch to appear to have lint failures pointing at non-existent files (ob-b7999514). In a separate task, a subagent's iterative variable rewrite left an `ineffassign` that `go vet` passed but golangci-lint caught, surfacing only at the lint gate (ob-2812d835).

payload.use_when: investigating CI failures on a feature branch, or starting a CI-repair task to fix a red pipeline
payload.content: Before diagnosing CI failures on a feature branch, check whether the failing file appears in the branch diff; failures in files absent from the diff indicate drift on the base branch, not a regression introduced by the branch. Before starting a CI-repair task, run each pipeline step independently (not through the serial `make check` shortcut) to get the true total scope — a pipeline that short-circuits on the first failure dramatically understates the real debt.
payload.causal_note: Pre-existing gofmt drift on main caused every descendant feature branch to show a red fmt-check gate on a file the branch never touched (ob-ca7460ad). Fixing only the gofmt layer in a serial pipeline then exposed ~54 golangci-lint errors that had been silently masked, causing scope to balloon mid-PR (ob-059fc00d).

payload.use_when: adding a new Go package to the monorepo, or committing test fixtures in a package with a testdata directory
payload.content: When creating a new Go package in the monorepo, immediately add a per-package gitignore entry for its in-place compiled binary (e.g., `auto-foo/auto`) — generic top-level patterns like `bin/` or `dist/` do not match binaries built inside package subdirectories. When a package needs committed test fixtures, add explicit negation entries for every distinct testdata subtree it uses (e.g., `!auto-graph/testdata/` AND `!auto-graph/e2e/testdata/`) — the repo-wide `**/testdata/` rule blocks all nested paths and a single top-level negation does not cascade.
payload.causal_note: A 42 MB compiled binary accumulated as untracked noise because generic gitignore patterns missed the in-place build location (ob-3d6c754c). In the same repo, committed e2e fixtures for both `testdata/` and `e2e/testdata/` were silently ignored by the root `**/testdata/` rule, causing CI to fail on a clean checkout while local tests passed (ob-ae40464b).

payload.use_when: creating a feature branch or git worktree, especially in the auto-stack monorepo where a pre-commit hook or daemon may advance main between sessions
payload.content: Before creating a feature branch or worktree, always run `git fetch origin && git push origin main` to confirm local main is fully in sync with origin. A local main that is ahead of origin — even by a few hook-generated commits — produces a PR diff polluted with unrelated commits that GitHub cannot auto-correct; recovery requires pushing main and patching the PR base via the GitHub API.
payload.causal_note: A worktree branched from a local main that was 3 commits ahead of origin caused 140+ unrelated files to appear in the PR diff (ob-1626dcf1). The auto-stack pre-commit hook and dogfooding daemon routinely advance main between sessions, making this a recurring risk.

payload.use_when: creating a worktree branch, rebasing a feature branch onto main, or working in a multi-agent environment where parallel PRs may be in flight
payload.content: Run `git fetch origin && git pull origin main` immediately before creating a worktree branch. After rebasing, run `git log origin/main..HEAD --oneline` and diff the incoming commits against your local changes — a parallel PR may have already landed the same fix, making your local production copy redundant; drop superseded hunks rather than carrying duplicates to the PR.
payload.causal_note: Forking from a stale local main causes mid-task rebase conflicts (ob-1a633a08: import-graph PR landed after worktree forked; ob-f9b834bb: planning-doc commit caused add/add rebase conflicts) and silent work duplication (ob-78ab4bf9: PR #112 merged the complete prune fix while the agent was re-implementing it, creating a conflicting PR).

payload.use_when: writing an implementation plan for a task, or about to open a PR on files that are also modified by other active tasks or dogfood agents
payload.content: Before writing an implementation plan, re-read every codebase file the plan will touch — do not rely solely on earlier planning docs. Before opening a PR, check `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD` on the hot files your task owns to detect in-flight commits from concurrent sessions; a parallel merge can land identical APIs with different names, producing hard conflicts at PR time.
payload.causal_note: ob-53f5c0ab: task 029 merged a central-store refactor after task 027 was planned, invalidating the entire plan mid-flight. ob-c4a34a79: a background dogfood session committed overlapping server changes (ConnectedPeers, project.list fan-out) to the same files while the feature worktree was executing the same work, causing a conflicting PR requiring manual merge-conflict resolution.

payload.use_when: emitting a stored git remote URL to any browser, bus event, log, or RPC response boundary
payload.content: Apply `git.NormalizeRemoteURL` defensively on every code path that emits a stored remote URL to a browser, bus, or log boundary — never assume the value in the registry is already credential-free. Any handler that re-emits stored registry data must normalize it itself, even if the writer appeared to normalize on insert.
payload.causal_note: ob-82ca803e: the `project.list` handler re-emitted stored registry remotes directly to the browser, leaking embedded credentials, because it trusted the stored value was already clean — unlike `FindProjectByRemote` which normalized both sides defensively.

payload.use_when: implementing any normalization, canonicalization, or sanitization function in Go
payload.content: Write an idempotence property test (f(f(x)) == f(x)) before hand-picking example inputs; author it first, before curated cases, because it reliably surfaces order-of-operations bugs — such as stripping a suffix before trimming surrounding characters that expose a second occurrence — that no fixed input set would reach.
payload.causal_note: Hand-picked inputs only cover anticipated orderings; idempotence violations reveal that the function's internal operation sequence is wrong, not just edge-case inputs — a class of bug that targeted tests systematically miss.

payload.use_when: executing a task that builds on a recently planned or recently merged upstream task, or dispatching subagents in a multi-phase epic pipeline
payload.content: Before creating the worktree and dispatching any subagent: (1) run `git log` to confirm each dependency task's merge commit is present; (2) run `go build ./...` in the affected module; (3) read the actual merged seam files (not task-doc descriptions) to extract true type and symbol names; (4) write one authoritative 'seam brief' shared by all phase subagents. If an upstream schema diverges from the design's stated contract, file a follow-up issue via `br create` scoped to that task and work around the gap — never expand the current task's scope to rewrite a sibling task's schema mid-execution. For epics where one task defines a schema consumed by another, author an integration-level contract test at the seam during the defining task's PR so field-shape mismatches are caught before the consuming task begins.
payload.causal_note: Planned symbol names in task docs are aspirational and guaranteed to differ from merged code; every subagent that starts without reading the real merged seams works with wrong type names, creating cascading adaptation overhead. Scope creep to fix a sibling schema ripples across multiple tasks and is a cross-task coordination call. Cross-task schema mismatches (e.g. named vs unnamed YAML sequences, bare paths vs URI strings) survive per-task CI and are only discovered when the downstream task is built.

payload.use_when: implementing or testing a stateful sync, render, or pipeline command that processes multi-step operation sequences
payload.content: Build a `rapid.StateMachine` model-based test alongside the implementation, not as a post-hoc regression gate; treat the first failing operation sequence as discovery of an undiscovered bug class and fix the implementation rather than constraining the model — targeted integration tests cannot observe pipeline-interaction bugs that emerge from operation ordering.
payload.causal_note: A targeted fix verified by integration tests can pass while leaving a second, more severe pipeline-interaction bug untouched; a state machine harness that generates arbitrary operation sequences (e.g. full-sync then scoped-sync) surfaces these ordering-dependent failures that fixed-sequence tests never reach.

payload.use_when: implementing or auditing a CLI verb that should apply/mutate/write data (e.g. update, sync, apply, prune, delete), or when a deletion command uses symbolic keys (style names, IDs, names) to locate targets
payload.content: Before closing any task that introduces a mutating CLI verb: (1) read the implementation of the engine function called and confirm it actually writes to disk — not just builds a plan — by checking whether it rewrites the lock file, materialises the commit, or renders targets; (2) for commands that delete or prune by symbolic key, trace the key through the write-path code (not the design doc) and confirm the key convention used at deletion time matches the key convention used at write time.
payload.causal_note: Prevents silent no-ops where acceptance tests pass vacuously: a plan-only engine sibling satisfies the literal criterion while writing nothing (ob-4cbd7ebc); a key convention mismatch causes an empty scan so the 'deletion succeeded' AC is trivially satisfied with nothing removed (ob-5626fb55).

payload.use_when: adding an explicit/fast-path branch alongside a default/walk branch, or shipping a new interface, resolver, or security gate whose tests use a fake or mock implementation
payload.content: When adding an explicit/fast-path branch: enumerate every normalization, deduplication, and validation step the default path runs and apply each one explicitly in the fast path too. When shipping a unit-tested interface or security gate with fake implementations: grep every production call site to confirm a real, non-nil implementation is constructed and passed; for security gates that take an allow-list parameter, verify the list is populated from project configuration at the call site — never left as nil.
payload.causal_note: Unit tests pass because fakes are wired correctly, but production silently skips the feature or gate: explicit path skips dedup causing last-writer-wins data corruption (ob-d140cd19); nil interface at production call site silently bypasses a deep-link feature (ob-f1593cc4); nil allow-list at the call site permanently disables a non-TTY/CI security opt-in gate (ob-0863c679).

payload.use_when: storing or comparing git URLs or file:// URIs as canonical identities, building a trust endpoint from a parsed URL, or detecting whether a filesystem path is a git repository root to record as a clonable source
payload.content: When storing a git source as a clonable URL: resolve the true repository root with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` and store any directory remainder as a separate Subpath field — never store the original subdirectory path as the clone target. When building a canonical identity string from a parsed URL: explicitly handle file:// (host is always the empty string; path carries the full identity) and write an isolated unit test for every supported URL scheme before shipping.
payload.causal_note: Storing a subdirectory as the clone URL produces an unclonable reference at sync time (ob-1fa243cb); using only the URL host component for file:// URLs collapses all local repositories to the same identity, silently granting cross-repository trust (ob-ef2262c4).

payload.use_when: writing new Go files in any auto-* package before the first commit, or renaming schema fields or config keys in a Go tool
payload.content: Apply these four checks before committing new Go code: (1) use `errors.New("literal message")` instead of `fmt.Errorf("literal message")` and direct string concatenation instead of `fmt.Sprintf("%s", x)` to satisfy the perfsprint linter; (2) check the zero-new-runtime-deps policy before importing any external library — verify stdlib covers the need first (e.g. `os.Stdin.Stat()` with `ModeCharDevice` for TTY detection rather than `golang.org/x/term`); (3) when the tool owns a YAML config file, parse it with `yaml.Decoder.KnownFields(true)` — the direct analog of `json.Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields()` — so unknown fields are rejected at load time; (4) after renaming any schema field or config key, run the full integration-test suite before committing, because doctor/validate commands embed field-name strings as literals that silently become stale.
payload.causal_note: Avoids a fixup-commit cycle: perfsprint failures surface at CI time instead of author time (ob-9af6d975); external dep import requires a full revert of go.mod/go.sum (ob-ee9c78d6); silent schema drift is caught at load time rather than at runtime with strict YAML parsing (ob-7f33ab32); stale field-name strings in doctor commands are the fastest class of breakage caught by integration tests (ob-4901891a).

payload.use_when: implementing a prune or GC command for a global shared cache, or implementing archive extraction that writes to a destination directory that may already contain files
payload.content: For global shared cache GC: build the referenced-IDs set by iterating the global project registry (e.g. `~/.auto/projects.json` via LoadProjects) — not just the current project's lock file — so entries still needed by other registered projects are never deleted. For archive extraction: replace `os.MkdirAll` with a component-by-component `Lstat` walk that rejects any symlink found along the path, including symlinks already present in the destination directory before extraction begins.
payload.causal_note: Using only the local lock file for a global prune deletes cache entries still needed by sibling projects, breaking their offline builds (ob-958c9fec); `os.MkdirAll` silently follows pre-existing symlinks in the destination, enabling directory traversal past the entry-validation boundary that was supposed to be the security perimeter (ob-b3c4f8b8).

payload.use_when: writing or reviewing a Go reconnect loop, reconcile manager, or connection watchdog in autowatch or auto-ui
payload.content: Bound every RPC or subscription call inside a reconnect/reconcile loop with context.WithTimeout. Model 'degraded' (transport up, post-connect setup failed) as a distinct state from 'disconnected' with its own bounded retry branch. Hook each connection's Serve/Read goroutine to atomically clear its liveness flag on exit so the next reconcile tick re-dials the slot rather than treating the closed peer as still-connected.
payload.causal_note: Without timeouts a non-responding peer permanently wedges the reconcile goroutine. Without a degraded state a subscribe-failed peer is never retried. Without clearing the liveness flag on Serve exit a dead peer is served indefinitely — all three bugs were found across the 042 and 045 tasks.

payload.use_when: designing a keepalive or peer-reap watchdog for any server-push or read-only subscriber protocol, or writing liveness/reap tests
payload.content: Design bidirectional ping/pong from the start for any protocol where clients are read-only consumers; a unidirectional server-ping watchdog cannot distinguish a dead peer from a healthy silent one on a reliable transport. For every positive 'dead peer reaped' assertion, add a bounded negative assertion that a healthy-but-app-idle peer survives past the same timeout, and make the dead simulation genuinely different from an idle peer — sever the connection or wedge reads, do not just go silent.
payload.causal_note: A unidirectional watchdog false-reaps healthy silent consumers (ob-0769b2d9). A silent-peer 'dead' simulation is behaviorally identical to a healthy read-only consumer, so a test asserting the watchdog fires proves the bug, not the intended behavior (ob-55a184e8).

payload.use_when: registering a shared handler struct or dispatcher onto multiple peer connections in an RPC or WebSocket server
payload.content: Never store per-connection state (subscription cancel func, session context, user identity, auth token) in a shared handler struct. Hold it exclusively in the accept-loop closure that owns the peer's lifetime. A single shared handler instance has no per-connection identity, so state written there is overwritten on each new connection.
payload.causal_note: A shared handler instance registered onto every peer caused subscription cancel funcs to be overwritten on each new connection, leaking subscriptions and making cancel impossible — found in the 040 event-ingest-relay task.

payload.use_when: creating events, records, or domain entities that are derived as a pure function of their inputs, especially when multiple independent code paths may derive the same logical item
payload.content: Assign deterministic IDs to any derived event or entity — e.g., a stable hash of source id + event type + relation — never random UUIDs. This ensures independently-produced copies of the same logical item collide on ID so a single dedup gate at any layer can suppress duplicates without per-path coordination.
payload.causal_note: Random IDs on derived events silently defeated consumer-side id-dedup: auto-ui's local /api/rpc derive and autowatch's derive both called NewEvent with a fresh random ID, so two doc.changed events passed the gate and consumers saw duplicates — found in the 045 task.

payload.use_when: designing or extending the RPC handler layer in autowatch or auto-ui, or adding new lifecycle or control-plane event types to the hub
payload.content: Keep RPC handlers thin: validate params, then delegate entirely to exported service methods. Emit lifecycle events (start, reap, cancel) from shared service primitives — e.g., startWorker/Reap — not from individual callers or dispatch paths. Gate control-plane events at the hub.Broadcast call site rather than at relay bridges so bridges can unconditionally forward everything on the hub without per-type filtering.
payload.causal_note: Fat handlers violate layering constraints and make unit tests hard. Caller-level emission duplicates or silently drops events when multiple paths exist (039 task). Relay-level gating scatters filtering logic and couples bridge code to event semantics (040 task).

payload.use_when: adding concurrency to a previously single-threaded daemon, introducing new package import relationships, or reimplementing an existing subsystem that has a reference implementation
payload.content: When adding concurrency to a single-threaded daemon, immediately add mutexes to all shared mutable state and prove correctness with go test -race before adding any other functionality — do not defer to a later retrofit. Encode package import constraints as executable layering tests (walk the dep graph with go list, fail on violations) rather than leaving them as documentation. When reimplementing an existing subsystem, write cross-surface parity tests that assert the new implementation's response shapes match the reference implementation before or alongside the code.
payload.causal_note: Concurrency retrofits are painful and introduce data races that ship undetected (039 task). Import violations found late require invasive refactors (039 task). Behavioral divergence from the reference — e.g., directory-walk ordering — is invisible to tests written only against the new code (038 task).

payload.use_when: implementing a localhost-bound HTTP handler that ingests events, hooks, or webhooks — especially when porting or adapting a guard from a sibling Go module's internal package
payload.content: Apply all three localhost ingest guards in order: (1) bind to loopback only, (2) reject any request that carries an Origin header (CSRF), (3) require Content-Type: application/json. When a reference implementation lives in a sibling module's internal package and cannot be imported, enumerate every guard from that source and re-implement each one explicitly — internal package boundaries mean no guard propagates automatically.
payload.causal_note: Loopback binding alone does not prevent CSRF: browsers can issue CORS-safelisted text/plain POSTs to 127.0.0.1 without triggering a preflight, so any page the user visits can forge events. Internal package semantics in Go prevent cross-module import, so guards that exist in one module's internal/ tree are silently absent when a new handler is created in another module unless the developer explicitly re-documents and re-implements them.

payload.use_when: consuming WebSocket messages, JSON-RPC notifications, or any typed event envelope in UI JavaScript or Go — especially when the event carries a nested data or params wrapper
payload.content: Never read payload fields directly off an envelope object (e.g. ev.path or params.path). Always route reads through a single typed parser function (e.g. parseDocChanged) that knows the exact nesting path. Pin the nesting contract with a backend serialization test so no consumer can silently regress when the envelope structure changes.
payload.causal_note: When WebSocket events nest the payload under ev.data and JSON-RPC notifications nest it under params.data, direct field access at the wrong level is always undefined — the subscription silently never matches, making liveness a no-op in production. A single parser function is the only reliable single source of truth for the correct access path.

payload.use_when: dispatching multiple subagents or parallel workers that share a single git worktree
payload.content: Dispatch subagents that share a worktree SERIALLY, not concurrently. After each phase, verify that the written files landed in the task worktree — not in main — by running `git -C <main-path> status` before dispatching the next phase.
payload.causal_note: Concurrent subagents sharing a worktree silently write into the PRIMARY worktree (main) instead of the task worktree, producing apparent 'lost writes' that are actually stale contamination of main. This has occurred on multiple tasks and is reliably triggered by parallel dispatch.

payload.use_when: writing conformance tests for auto-ui or any no-build browser SPA in this repo
payload.content: For auto-ui changes, write browser-driven conformance harnesses that assert `data-*` DOM attributes and `window.__autoui` counters rather than rendered text; after poll-to-settle, assert the rendered DOM value directly — not only a side-effect counter that fires regardless of whether the view re-rendered; avoid JavaScript eval expressions that return strings containing multibyte Unicode and use boolean predicates instead (e.g., `element !== null`). Never rely on `go build`/`go test` alone to validate frontend correctness.
payload.causal_note: `go build`/`go test` pass through real frontend defects (stale closures, missing reactive updates, wrong selectors); rendered text can be textually identical before and after a fetch while internal state has changed; side-effect counters advance even when the component shows stale data; multibyte Unicode eval expressions return byte counts rather than string values.

payload.use_when: adding a callback, sink, or handler func field to a Go struct whose goroutine may be started before the field is assigned
payload.content: Never store a mutable callback or event-sink as a plain `func` field on a struct whose Run goroutine can start before the field is wired; store it in `atomic.Value`, load it into a local variable per invocation, and invoke the local copy outside any existing mutex.
payload.causal_note: Assigning a plain func field after goroutine start is a data race detected by the Go race detector; invoking a callback while holding a mutex risks lock-order inversion with any mutex the callback itself acquires.

payload.use_when: writing or refactoring auto-ui event handlers, subscribe-on-mount hooks (useEffect with [] deps), or removing a write-only state mirror
payload.content: Pass only stable module-level selectors to subscribe-on-mount hooks — never a closure that captures a component prop; key the component on the prop if a prop-parameterised selector is needed. When an event handler gates on a narrow condition (e.g., `!known`), explicitly verify whether known-path or already-seen-resource updates also need handling before shipping. Before deleting a write-only state mirror, enumerate every field it carried and prove each field survives under the replacement model, including param-less routes that may inadvertently re-derive and clear state.
payload.causal_note: A prop-closing selector captured at mount time becomes stale after subsequent prop changes with no runtime error; a too-narrow event guard produces silent stale UI; deleting a state mirror silently breaks any field that relied on its structural persistence.

payload.use_when: writing conformance specs for reactive auto-ui components, or designing bus-event conformance tests that use `auto ui emit`
payload.content: In each acceptance criterion for a reactive UI component, add an explicit note on what triggers an update (page load, reconnect, event-driven, or reload-required) and what does NOT update autonomously; before designing bus-event conformance tests, verify `auto ui emit` supports the required event types and envelope fields, and if it does not, document the `curl /api/rpc` workaround with its exact CloudEvents envelope shape in the conformance spec.
payload.causal_note: Omitting update-trigger boundaries leads to false test assertions that the UI updates autonomously when it actually requires a reload; relying on `auto ui emit` without checking its capabilities leads to fragile manual curl workarounds that silently emit malformed envelopes.

payload.use_when: writing agent-browser conformance tests that trigger interactions on a reactive SPA or fire WebSocket events
payload.content: After any interaction that triggers a re-render — including WebSocket events, navigation, or clicks — re-snapshot the page with `snapshot -i` before issuing the next `click @ref` or attribute read. For WebSocket-driven updates, poll the observable attribute with a 2–3 s timeout rather than reading it once; HTTP 204 from the emitter confirms only server receipt, not client render completion.
payload.causal_note: Prevents two categories of flaky failures: stale agent-browser snapshot refs that silently drop clicks (misdiagnosed as product logic bugs), and single-read assertions that race the Hub → WS → client handler → framework re-render propagation chain.

payload.use_when: developing or testing a no-build browser SPA served by Go's http.FileServer with an esm.sh import map
payload.content: Apply three non-negotiable disciplines for no-build Preact/esm.sh SPAs: (1) prefix every transitive import-map entry with `*` (e.g. `"preact/hooks": "https://esm.sh/*preact@10.x.x/hooks"`) so nested imports inside esm.sh-fetched modules route back through the map and do not produce duplicate framework instances; (2) wrap `http.FileServer` in middleware that injects `Cache-Control: no-store` so browsers do not replay cached ES modules after a server change; (3) treat the browser conformance step as a mandatory acceptance gate — Go unit tests are structurally incapable of catching module-resolution, import-map, or HTTP-caching failures.
payload.causal_note: All three gaps produced blank-page or silently-broken regressions that `go test` reported as passing: duplicate Preact instances broke stateful hooks with no error, cached modules hid server changes visible only to curl, and module-resolution failures were invisible to Go tests but broke every user-visible AC.

payload.use_when: adding mount-time RPC calls to any auto-ui component, or changing the SPA's default landing view to one that fetches on mount
payload.content: Add a `whenOpen(): Promise<void>` readiness gate in rpc.js that delays mount-time fetches until the WebSocket is OPEN; call.() must not reject synchronously while the socket is still CONNECTING. When a component that makes RPC calls on mount becomes the default landing view, add a cold-load conformance assertion that verifies data arrives on first page open without a manual reload.
payload.causal_note: Prevents a deterministic cold-load failure where every mount-time RPC call rejects with 'not connected' until the user manually reloads. The bug is latent while the landing view makes no mount-time calls and surfaces immediately when any component that fetches on mount is promoted to the default route.

payload.use_when: writing code that prefix-matches, correlates by text, or serializes a field that has both a full-length and a truncated/preview variant (e.g. session intent, commit message body, any preview column in a list row vs a detail row)
payload.content: Always fetch the full-length variant of a text field when performing prefix or substring matching — never use the truncated list-row preview. When both forms appear in CLI JSON output, give each a distinct key name (e.g. `first_user_intent` for the full value, `first_user_intent_preview` for the truncated one) so consumers cannot silently receive different shapes under one key.
payload.causal_note: ob-4b47b9aa: sub-agent correlation by prompt-prefix silently broke for any child session whose intent exceeded 200 chars because the preview from SessionListRow was used instead of the full string from GetSessionByID. ob-7425655f: `session list` and `session describe` both emitted `first_user_intent` but with incompatible lengths, making downstream parsing non-deterministic depending on which command the consumer called.

payload.use_when: writing test fixtures for pairing-based logic (tool_use_id, foreign-key joins), token/byte budget bound assertions, or directory-tree distance label assertions in auto-search or auto-etl
payload.content: For pairing-based fixture rows, always include a complete originator+result pair — a standalone result row with no matching originator is silently skipped and gives false confidence that the code path is exercised. For budget/token assertions, generate the fixture first and measure the actual output size empirically, then set the bound. For tree-distance fixtures, compute every d-label arithmetically (d = up-segments-to-LCA + down-segments-from-LCA, basenames stripped from both paths) before writing assertions.
payload.causal_note: ob-f16f47c1: a standalone role=tool Bash row with no tool_use_id was silently skipped by the builder, making the AC appear covered when it was a no-op. ob-eb6285e9: an initial hot-file fixture produced only 395 tokens under --all (below the 500 bound it was meant to exceed), so the passing assertion was vacuous. ob-72b37b7e: a one-level-shallow seed shifted all d-labels by one, causing incorrect fixture assertions that propagated silently.

payload.use_when: embedding arbitrary Go-marshalled JSON into an HTML <script> block — in any template or string-builder that injects model data into a page
payload.content: Never use Go's default json.Marshal to produce JSON for <script> injection. Always: (1) create an encoder with SetEscapeHTML(false), (2) explicitly replace every `</` with `<\/` and every U+2028/U+2029 with their escape sequences in the resulting bytes, and (3) make this a standalone tested helper function — not an inline ad-hoc step.
payload.causal_note: ob-0a7c6a11: Go's default HTML-escape mode silently corrupts JSON containing `</script>`, breaking page parsing. The fix requires both disabling HTML escape AND explicit `</` replacement, because SetEscapeHTML(false) alone still leaves U+2028/U+2029 line separators that break script context.

payload.use_when: writing SQL or Go that joins across ETL datasets (commits, git_refs, messages, sessions) or builds a lookup by commit SHA across the global dataset in auto-etl or auto-search
payload.content: Before writing a join on any cross-table key, read the source code that writes each side and verify the exact stored format — do not rely on prose documentation. For commit SHA joins: always scope by git_remote first, then match via full-SHA prefix comparison (stored value starts-with the abbreviation), never by exact stored-ID equality. Write a test asserting the join returns at least one row against a known fixture.
payload.causal_note: ob-f21f364c: `git-history-etl.md` described `commits.id` as a plain SHA while the code writes `<repoID>-<sha>`; the resulting join returned zero rows at runtime but passed build and linting. ob-2b590bba: git abbreviates output to 7 chars while stored IDs may be 8 or 40; exact equality plus missing repo-scope caused missed lookups and cross-repo false positives.

payload.use_when: writing table-rendering or CLI output formatting code that displays data from columns that may contain embedded newlines — commit message bodies, tool output, file content snippets
payload.content: Sanitize embedded newlines inside the lowest-level single-responsibility formatting helper (e.g. a `truncSubject` or `formatCell` function), not at individual call sites. Include at least one fixture value with an embedded newline in the test suite — if every fixture uses single-line values, the rendering bug survives CI but fires on the first real record with a body.
payload.causal_note: ob-7995e7c5: every test fixture used single-line commit subjects, so the multi-line-breaks-row bug was invisible in CI; it would have fired on the first real commit with a body. Fixing inside `truncSubject` protected all future callers automatically versus a call-site fix that would have left new callers unprotected.

payload.use_when: adding a new value to an enumerated set (message roles, tool kinds, status codes) that has validator functions in multiple packages, or adding rows to a test fixture that is shared across multiple test files in auto-search
payload.content: Consolidate duplicated value-whitelist functions into a single shared package-level constant or function — never maintain parallel copies across packages. When a test fixture is shared across multiple test files, centralise any absolute-count assertion in a single constant or helper, or switch to relative assertions (`got == before+N`) so that adding fixture rows requires exactly one change.
payload.causal_note: ob-5a62123d: `normalizeRole` existed independently in `search/messages.go` and `stats/validate.go`; adding `thinking` to one copy while missing the other caused `stats --role thinking` to be rejected on the missed path. ob-7513761b: adding 4 fixture rows to exercise a new code path required hunting and updating more than 10 hard-coded count assertions spread across 5 test files.

payload.use_when: adding registry-based filtering to a Go ETL command or CLI tool that reads the project registry to decide which repos to process
payload.content: Gate registry filtering at the cmd layer where both path and remote are available; pass gated slices/maps to internal packages and keep those packages registry-agnostic. Use a quiet read-only load (stat + LoadProjects, return empty on error) rather than EnsureProjects, which mutates the registry as a side effect of being called. payload.use_when: writing acceptance criteria for an exclusion or filtering gate, or auditing a plan after a design decision has changed (e.g., a parameter removed, shared logic relocated)
payload.content: Before accepting an exclusion gate's AC, trace at least one concrete instance of the thing to exclude through every 'keep' branch of the condition — the task's own Problem statement is the best counterexample. After any design decision resolves, audit all function signatures, test file names, and import lists in the plan for stale references before implementation begins; Go silently accepts unused function parameters, so a dead registry arg in an Ingest signature compiles and ships without warning.
