payload.use_when: writing Go tests for ETL transforms, especially negative-path assertions or comparisons between two systems that store data in different formats
payload.content: For negative-path assertions, write `if badConditionHolds { t.Error(...) }` — never `if !condition { t.Log("ok") }`, which is a no-op on the failure path and will always pass. For cross-system format comparisons (e.g., SSH vs HTTPS remote URLs, flat vs partitioned parquet paths), feed each side of the assertion its actual production-format value; pre-normalizing both inputs to the same format hides the format-mismatch bug that only exists in production.
payload.causal_note: An inverted `!condition + t.Log` assertion passed regardless of whether the invariant was violated, caught only by automated PR review; pre-normalized test inputs for SSH/HTTPS URL comparison made tests pass while production code silently failed on the format difference (ob-c821f403 high-severity, ob-cca3fa9e across two sessions).

payload.use_when: implementing a --full rebuild flag for an ETL source that has its own external sync-state file, or writing a fixture-generation script that invokes an incremental ETL tool
payload.content: Wire `--full` to delete ALL incremental state for the source — including external sync-state files (e.g., `~/.auto/etl/git/sync-state.json`) — not only the output directory. For fixture-generation scripts, run the ETL tool under an isolated temp HOME so no pre-existing sync-state file suppresses output on developer machines that have already indexed the target dataset.
payload.causal_note: A --full flag that only removed the output dir left the seen-SHA set intact, causing every commit to be treated as already-seen and producing zero rows with no error — indistinguishable from a successful incremental run; fixture scripts sharing the developer's HOME produced partial or empty snapshots on machines with prior state (ob-2fdc70d0, ob-4d6ac5f6 across two sessions).

payload.use_when: adding a new Go dependency to one sub-module inside a go.work monorepo
payload.content: Run `go mod tidy` only in the specific sub-module directory that needs the new dependency; do not edit go.work or run a workspace-level tidy — the go.work.sum is updated automatically on the next workspace build or CI merge, and there is no replace/require conflict to pre-empt unless go.work already pins that module explicitly.
payload.causal_note: Prevents unnecessary go.work churn and merge conflicts; editing go.work for a sub-module-scoped dependency is a no-op at best and a conflict source at worst, and forgetting the sub-module tidy leaves the go.sum stale, breaking builds in CI.

payload.use_when: writing Go code that reads JSONL or line-delimited records, globs for files, or walks directory trees containing parquet partitions
payload.content: Never use filepath.Glob with ** patterns (Go does not support recursive glob; use filepath.WalkDir with a suffix filter instead). Never use bufio.Scanner for records that may exceed 64KB (use bufio.Reader.ReadBytes('\n') instead). Both APIs fail silently: Glob returns zero results, Scanner silently drops or errors on long lines. Write fixture tests with the same nested directory structure that production data uses.
payload.causal_note: filepath.Glob ** silently returned zero partitions in production parquet walks while flat-fixture tests passed (ob-1d723039). bufio.Scanner silently dropped 1 MiB hook-event lines; even scanner.Buffer(1MiB, 1MiB) was insufficient once an envelope wrapper pushed the line past the cap (ob-c90d58a1). Both are high-severity silent correctness failures that do not surface until E2E tests or real data are used.

payload.use_when: reading a git remote URL to store in parquet, a log file, a JSON event, or any other persistent format
payload.content: Always call StripCredentials() (or equivalent) on every git remote URL before writing it to any output format — parquet, JSONL, JSON, logs. The spec will not mention credential stripping; apply it defensively at the normalize layer, not at individual call sites, so it cannot be skipped.
payload.causal_note: git remote get-url origin returned x-access-token:github_pat_...@github.com URLs that flowed unstripped into both repo_remote and repo_remote_normalized parquet columns (ob-11620ba6). Only E2E testing against a real repo caught the leak before ship. Specs consistently omit this requirement.

payload.use_when: adding, removing, or renaming columns in an ETL parquet schema, or abandoning a feature branch that wrote parquet partitions
payload.content: Default new tool-output or envelope columns to a single raw JSON TEXT/STRING parquet field rather than typed per-field columns; this isolates the schema from upstream format changes and lets DuckDB json_extract handle derived analytics. When typed schema changes are unavoidable, bump model.SchemaVersion on any branch that emits new columns and revert or re-ingest orphaned partitions before abandoning the branch — DuckDB NULL-fill silently hides cross-partition column drift until a full --full backfill is required.
payload.causal_note: An abandoned branch left orphaned columns (tool_use_id, duration_ms, interrupted) in one weekly partition; DuckDB hid the drift invisibly in normal queries, requiring a full backfill to remediate (ob-51432633). Typed envelope columns lock the schema to whatever the producer emits today, so any field addition triggers cross-partition drift on future changes (ob-9e9f39df).

payload.use_when: designing or extending a producer/ETL pipeline where raw capture logs may be collected or replayed from multiple hosts
payload.content: Store in the producer-side capture envelope ALL fields the ETL host cannot safely re-derive: working directory, project registry lookups, host identity, and row IDs derived from the producer's HostID. Never let ETL re-resolve these fields; it will silently substitute ETL-host values and produce host-unstable IDs that break crash-idempotent dedup in shared parquet datasets. Apply this check uniformly — any field whose justification is 'the ETL host may differ from the producer' must live in the envelope.
payload.causal_note: Task 022 correctly stored cwd in the envelope for multi-host safety but left project for ETL re-resolution, the identical hazard. Row IDs derived from the ETL-process hostID were not stable across hosts, breaking dedup in shared parquet datasets (ob-72d2bd7a). The same argument (ETL host != producer host) applies to every such field, so a systematic envelope audit is required.

payload.use_when: implementing a multi-stage pipeline with a scanner phase and a separate consumer/builder phase (e.g. file-walker + graph builder, AST scanner + context-pack builder) in the auto-graph or any auto-* package
payload.content: Define all cross-stage constants (import-kind names, edge labels, skip-path lists) in one shared package imported by both producer and consumer; add a canonicalization shim at the boundary if the producer is external or legacy; and require at least one integration test that exercises the full path from real scanner output through the consumer — never rely on synthetic unit tests alone at this seam.
payload.causal_note: String literal mismatches between scanner and builder, divergent skip lists between the file-walker and scanner, and synthetic unit tests with auto-generated goldens all produce silently wrong output (zero-edge graphs, misclassified edges, hidden interface bugs) with no error signal — only an integration test using real scanner output surfaces them.

payload.use_when: parsing structured config or data files (JSONC, go.mod, tsconfig.json, YAML) line-by-line or via regex transformation to extract values or strip non-standard syntax
payload.content: Strip inline comments and unquote values as the first step before field extraction; if transforming structured text (e.g. stripping JSONC comments), implement a single-pass state machine that tracks whether the cursor is inside a string rather than chaining independent regex passes over the same text.
payload.causal_note: A two-pass regex approach (strip comments then strip trailing commas) matches structural patterns inside string values and silently corrupts data; naive line parsing that ignores inline comments or quoted module paths silently produces zero-edge or empty graphs with no error.

payload.use_when: adding a new EdgeKind to the auto-graph shared edge model, or adding a validation/budget check in any auto-* pipeline that operates on incrementally-built objects
payload.content: When adding a new edge kind, audit every adjacency-map builder and traversal loop for EdgeKind filters — unfiltered iteration with lenient attribute fallbacks silently misclassifies the new kind; when enforcing any budget or validation threshold, call the object's full materialization/refresh step (all derived sections populated) before the check — checking a partial model produces a systematically optimistic estimate.
payload.causal_note: Existing adjacency-map iteration without EdgeKind filtering misclassified doc-link edges as import dependencies; a context-pack budget enforcer run before relationships and guidance sections were populated accepted too many candidates and caused overruns in the final output.

payload.use_when: writing or reviewing ast-grep patterns for TypeScript or TSX import scanning
payload.content: When using ast-grep on TypeScript projects, always invoke it twice — once with `--lang=ts` and once with `--lang=tsx` — and merge the results; additionally, use `$$$` (not `$_`) wherever a list of nodes can appear (destructuring, re-export braces, argument lists), because `$_` matches exactly one node and silently misses multi-item occurrences.
payload.causal_note: A single `--lang=ts` pass silently drops all imports inside `.tsx` files with no error or warning; separately, patterns using `$_` in list positions silently miss every multi-name re-export — both failures produce incomplete graphs that appear correct until unit tests catch them.

payload.use_when: writing Go config accessor functions (Get, Read, Quietly variants) or OS-bootstrapped init helpers such as EnsureHost
payload.content: Config accessor functions for constrained values (host IDs, tokens, format-validated strings) must validate the stored value against the same format regex used at write time, not merely check for emptiness — a missing value is an expected error, but an invalid format silently returned is a data-corruption bug. EnsureHost-style init helpers must treat each OS API call as independently failable: generate the composite default only when all calls succeed, fall back to a bare hostname if user.Current() fails, and fall back further if even the bare value fails format validation.
payload.causal_note: A 'quiet' accessor that skips regex validation allows hand-edited invalid config to propagate silently onto bus events or outbound API calls. Composite hostname+username defaults silently break in containerized environments where /etc/passwd is absent.

payload.use_when: Collapsing or single-sourcing two duplicated Go functions (counters, scope-keying helpers, normalization callers) into a shared implementation
payload.content: Before collapsing two duplicated implementations into one shared function: (1) enumerate every axis on which the two callers differed — scope flags, normalization chains, universe bounds — and make each an explicit parameter of the shared function; (2) verify both call sites run the identical normalization chain end-to-end, not just the same entry-point symbol. A partial normalization shortcut in one copy produces silent divergence only on non-canonical inputs that pass all existing tests.
payload.causal_note: Omitting a normalization step in one copy caused a 390-vs-396 count mismatch on .git-suffixed remotes (ob-f245ee59). Omitting the scope flag axis from the shared function caused a --all pending-universe regression visible only to the callers that relied on it (ob-1418e580).

payload.use_when: planning removal or deletion of a CLI command, HTTP route, or internal interface, or when an executor encounters a deletion that was not explicitly scoped in the plan
payload.content: Before scheduling deletion of a CLI command or HTTP route, grep all source files (including CLI command files, test helpers, and doc strings) for the path or command name and enumerate every consumer explicitly in scope or call them out as out-of-scope decisions. If execution uncovers an unplanned removal of a user-visible CLI surface, halt immediately, surface the fork with options (remove / retarget / defer to a separate task) and rationale, and await explicit authorization before proceeding — CLI removals are irreversible API changes.
payload.causal_note: ob-e53a77b4: a plan to delete an HTTP route missed `auto ui emit` (a CLI command that POST'd to the same route); it only surfaced at deletion time when tests failed, blocking the gate and forcing an unplanned mid-execution decision. ob-2d0d93f3: an executor correctly halted when it discovered a user-visible command removal that was not in its authorization, presented options, and waited — proceeding unilaterally would have been an irreversible API change.

payload.use_when: writing Go helper functions intended for use in a subsequent commit, or planning multi-phase Go implementation commits
payload.content: Never commit Go helper functions as an isolated phase ahead of their callers; always include the consuming call sites in the same commit so that the unused-symbol lint check in the pre-commit hook passes on every intermediate state.
payload.causal_note: ob-f9820760: committing resolveRoot, cleanDocPath, and other helpers before their callers caused `unused` lint failures in the pre-commit hook; the only fix was to merge the isolated helpers commit with the consuming phase into a single commit.

payload.use_when: context.md or a plan references APIs or symbols from a dependency that was marked 'planned' or 'not yet merged' at planning time
payload.content: At execution start, grep for every symbol the plan references from 'planned-not-merged' dependencies; read the actual merged files and adapt to the real signatures before writing any code. The implementation contract is what matters, not the identifier that was planned against.
payload.causal_note: Context docs snapshot planned APIs at planning time; the moment those dependencies merge, the snapshot becomes stale. Executors who trust the plan discover wrong signatures mid-implementation (e.g. `skill.ParseLock` taking `[]byte` instead of a loader package, `sync.Run` vs the planned `sync.Update`), forcing silent adaptation or re-architecture.

payload.use_when: preparing to close or mark a task complete, especially tasks that are part of a larger epic
payload.content: Before closing a task, explicitly check each acceptance criterion in plan.html against what actually shipped in the code; do not rely on the absence of failing tests as proof of completeness — features with no test coverage can silently omit planned scope and only surface during a downstream epic audit.
payload.causal_note: A task can ship only part of its planned scope (e.g. the host-field portion of an epic that also defined a ctl.* event namespace) and be marked complete because nothing breaks. The missing scope then becomes a hidden gap discovered much later, requiring unplanned follow-up work.

payload.use_when: scripting any CLI command inside a plan step, acceptance criterion, or rollout note
payload.content: Before writing any CLI subcommand into a plan step or AC rollout note, run `<binary> --help` (or `<binary> <subcommand> --help`) to confirm the exact subcommand name and required flags. Never infer subcommand names from the binary name, package name, or a similar project's conventions.
payload.causal_note: Planning docs that reference a non-existent subcommand (e.g., `autoetl transform` when the real surface is `autoetl run`) cause every downstream E2E verification step to fail as written, forcing unplanned rework during execution (ob-daad82b6).

payload.use_when: about to call the Edit tool on any file
payload.content: Always call Read on a file before calling Edit in the same session. The Edit tool enforces this sequencing constraint and will raise an immediate error if Read was skipped, requiring an extra round-trip before the write can proceed.
payload.causal_note: Skipping Read before Edit is a hard tool invariant: the edit is blocked until Read is run, wasting a full round-trip (ob-3276644c). In long agentic chains this compounds latency and can break sequencing assumptions downstream.

payload.use_when: writing a Go test that must simulate a stale Unix socket — a socket file present on disk with no live server behind it
payload.content: Use net.ListenUnix with ln.SetUnlinkOnClose(false) to keep the socket path on disk after the listener is closed. Do not use net.Listen("unix", path) — it auto-unlinks the socket file on close, making stale-file simulation impossible and producing a false pass or wrong behavior.
payload.causal_note: Go's net.Listen("unix", ...) removes the socket file on close, so tests written with it found no file and either false-passed or exercised a completely different code path than the stale-socket scenario they were designed to cover.

payload.use_when: planning or executing a refactor phase that deletes a Go test file
payload.content: Before deleting a test file, check whether it contains TestMain or any package-level variable (e.g. testBinaryPath) referenced by other test files in the same package. If so, relocate those symbols to a neutral helper file (e.g. helpers_test.go) in the same atomic step — never leave a gap across separate phases where the package is uncompilable.
payload.causal_note: Deleting e2e_feedback_test.go removed TestMain and a shared build variable that other test files in the same package still referenced, silently breaking compilation for the entire test package between the deletion step and the replacement step in a later phase.

payload.use_when: golangci-lint reports findings at file paths that no longer exist on disk, or after removing a sibling worktree while another branch is active
payload.content: When `golangci-lint` reports findings whose file paths point at a non-existent directory or a removed sibling worktree, run `golangci-lint cache clean` before re-running lint; treat the original findings as stale cache artifacts rather than real defects on the current branch.
payload.causal_note: golangci-lint maintains a shared on-disk cache that retains analysis entries for files from deleted worktrees, producing phantom CI-blocking failures on what is actually a clean branch — as in ob-f2c8b167 where gosec findings referenced a non-existent `auto-stack-task-016/` directory.

payload.use_when: writing or reviewing acceptance criteria that include e2e test coverage, or authoring e2e tests with performance assertions
payload.content: Acceptance criteria that require e2e coverage must explicitly state the build-tag-aware invocation (e.g., `go test -tags=e2e ./e2e/`); `go test ./...` silently skips files guarded by `//go:build e2e`, making e2e ACs vacuously passable. Performance timing assertions in e2e tests must wrap only the production code path under measurement — test setup steps (repo clone, binary compile) must complete before the timer starts, or the assertion measures infrastructure, not the target operation.
payload.causal_note: An e2e AC citing only `go test ./...` was passable without ever running the e2e suite because the tests were behind a `//go:build e2e` tag (ob-03798936). A performance assertion that included clone and compile time would be network/toolchain-dependent rather than measuring the operation it claimed to test (ob-51b8d087). Both were in the same codebase.

payload.use_when: merging a PR with `gh pr merge` from inside a linked worktree, or scripting the merge step of `complete-task`
payload.content: After running `gh pr merge` from a linked worktree, verify success via `gh pr view --json state,mergedAt` rather than trusting the command's exit code; the merge succeeds on GitHub but the local checkout step fails with `'main' is already used by worktree`, causing a non-zero exit that can mislead an agent into retrying an already-merged PR.
payload.causal_note: ob-5469b219: the merge succeeded on GitHub but `gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch` exited non-zero because the primary checkout already held main, which is a normal worktree constraint, not a merge failure.

payload.use_when: staging a large batch of auto-generated or mechanical files for a commit while needing to exclude one or a few specific files
payload.content: Stage a large batch while excluding specific files with `git add -A && git reset -q -- <excluded-file>` rather than individually enumerating hundreds of paths; the excluded files remain cleanly unstaged and can be committed separately with their own message.
payload.causal_note: ob-2e12b7ca: individually staging 167 mechanical files is error-prone; the add-then-reset pattern reliably commits the batch while leaving real-content edits in a distinct commit.

payload.use_when: writing E2E or unit test fixtures for code paths that shell out to git (e.g. `git ls-files`, `git log`)
payload.content: For E2E fixtures that exercise code paths which shell out to git, initialize them as real git repos (`git init && git add -A && git commit -m 'init'`). For unit test fixtures validating the same code, use a plain non-git directory to assert the soft-failure / graceful-degradation path; keep the two fixture types in separate directories to make the distinction explicit.
payload.causal_note: ob-c505c735: E2E tests for auto-graph doc-links failed because the fixture directory was not a git repo, causing `git ls-files` to return nothing; the unit test fixture deliberately used a non-git dir to test the degradation path, so the two concerns needed separate fixture trees.

payload.use_when: writing property-based tests in Go against validated schemas, regex-constrained identifiers, or tightly constrained input spaces
payload.content: Use constructive generators that assemble valid inputs by composition over constrained schemas; never add rejection filters or restrict generator ranges to make a failing property pass — instead, stop at the first shrunk counterexample, report it, and explicitly document and scope out any known-impossible inputs with a named exclusion comment.
payload.causal_note: Rejection-based generators over constrained spaces exhaust their quota and silently stop exploring; narrowing a generator to avoid a failure ships a false-green test that proves nothing and masks a genuine bug the property exposed.

payload.use_when: writing a CLI command that resolves a user-supplied name, identifier, or path argument to a filesystem location
payload.content: Validate every user-supplied identifier against its canonical name regex (e.g. `^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$`) before constructing any `filepath.Join` call; reject the request with a clear error if the identifier contains `..`, `/`, or any separator character.
payload.causal_note: Passing a raw CLI argument directly into filepath.Join allows path-traversal attacks — e.g. `auto skill get ../../../tmp/leak --target claude` reads SKILL.md files outside the managed skills tree with no indication of the escape.

payload.use_when: calling a Go engine or pipeline function that may record partial failures in a result struct rather than surfacing them as a returned Go error
payload.content: After calling any engine or pipeline function that returns both a Go error and a result struct, always check `err` AND `result.ExitCode()`/`result.Errors` before emitting a success message or returning zero; never gate the success path on the Go error alone.
payload.causal_note: Partial-failure pipeline functions routinely return a nil Go error while recording planning, fetch, or render failures inside the result struct; checking only `err` causes exit-0 with errors silently omitted — e.g. an invalid repo URL prints 'All skills are up to date.' instead of failing.

payload.use_when: writing or extending HTTP handler tests for a handler that validates request headers (Content-Type, Origin, Authorization, etc.)
payload.content: In HTTP handler test helpers, always set every header that a conformant client would send — including Content-Type and any auth headers — from the very first test case. Adding a new header-validation guard must only require adding negative test cases, not retrofitting every existing test.
payload.causal_note: Tests written without required headers become mechanically broken the moment a corresponding validation guard is added. Every existing test then needs a retrofit instead of only a new negative case, increasing churn and risk of missing a regression.

payload.use_when: writing shell install or update scripts that run under `set -euo pipefail` and perform a post-install side-effect after the critical step has already succeeded (daemon restart, cache invalidation, service reload)
payload.content: Guard every post-install side-effect command with `|| true` or an explicit `if … ; then … else echo 'warning: …' >&2; fi` block so that a transient failure degrades to a logged warning rather than aborting the script with a non-zero exit and misleading the user into thinking the primary step failed.
payload.causal_note: When a daemon restart issued after a successful binary replacement fails transiently, `set -euo pipefail` aborts the whole script. The binary was already updated, but the user sees an error exit and believes the update failed — a false overall failure caused by a non-critical side effect.

payload.use_when: writing E2E or integration tests that expect events produced by multiple concurrent senders or connections
payload.content: When an E2E test expects events from multiple concurrent senders, collect all expected event IDs into a set and loop until the set is complete; never assert sequential arrival order across concurrent connections.
payload.causal_note: `readUntil`-style sequential reads silently discard events that arrive out of order across concurrent connections, producing nondeterministic test failures where the second expected event is lost because it arrived before the first was consumed.

payload.use_when: implementing or reviewing a proxy layer that decodes routing selectors from JSON or performs format conversion between upstream and downstream contracts
payload.content: In a proxy routing decoder, enumerate every field-name alias documented in the protocol spec (both camelCase and snake_case variants) and add an explicit test for each alias; perform format conversions (e.g., base64 → raw bytes) inside the proxy layer so the client-facing contract stays byte-identical; for RPC proxy unit tests, inject a DialFunc backed by `net.Pipe` peers rather than real sockets to achieve full API-level coverage without binding ports or spawning subprocesses.
payload.causal_note: A missing alias silently routes all requests using the documented name to the wrong backend with no error; leaving format conversion to the client forces unnecessary client-side changes and breaks the documented contract; real-socket tests add subprocess/port overhead that `net.Pipe` eliminates.

payload.use_when: writing shell conformance scripts that call `agent-browser eval` to inspect or assert on DOM state
payload.content: In `agent-browser eval` shell calls: (1) always pipe string output through `tr -d '"'` before comparison or grep, because the tool JSON-encodes string return values with surrounding double-quotes; (2) avoid multi-statement JS with `const`/`let` declarations, which fail silently through shell interpolation — use single property-chain expressions (`(el || {}).prop`) instead.
payload.causal_note: Prevents two classes of silent false-pass: the first causes assertions to miss correct DOM values because the JSON-wrapped `"value"` never matches the bare `value` being compared; the second causes the eval to silently return the else-branch when the element exists but the JS block scope is mangled by shell quoting.

payload.use_when: writing liveness or invalidation-driven conformance tests for auto-ui, especially tests that emit `doc.changed` or similar bus events
payload.content: Before emitting an invalidation signal, write the backing resource to disk (or to the store) first — the emit only posts the envelope and does not modify backing state, so a re-fetch will find nothing new if the resource is absent. When asserting monotonic render counters (data-revision, nonce, sequence numbers), snapshot the value before triggering the event and assert strictly-greater-than the snapshot rather than an absolute expected value.
payload.causal_note: Prevents silent false-passes: an invalidation event with no backing resource causes the re-list to find nothing new, and a monotonic counter starting from a non-zero baseline (left by earlier navigation) will never equal the hardcoded absolute value asserted.

payload.use_when: implementing any RPC or HTTP handler in auto-ui (or any auto-* server) that accepts a filesystem path from the client
payload.content: Validate every client-supplied filesystem path against a known project registry allowlist before passing it to any filesystem operation, even when the server listens on loopback only. Loopback scope does not eliminate path-traversal risk — an unvalidated worktree path can be used to read arbitrary host files.
payload.causal_note: A `doc.get`/`doc.list` handler that accepted an arbitrary worktree path without registry validation would allow any local process to read any host file via the RPC surface. Loopback-only binding is not a security boundary for path-traversal.

payload.use_when: designing a two-binary producer/consumer system where both binaries need to parse or normalize the same file format or event envelope
payload.content: Before writing either binary, identify all normalization and extraction logic that both sides need and place it in a shared internal module (e.g., auto-shared); never define shared logic in package main, as it cannot be imported by any other module and silently forces the consuming binary to re-implement it.
payload.causal_note: auto-cli's `extractPaths`, `stringField`, and `buildHookEvent` lived in package main, so auto-etl could not import them; the ETL 'reuse' claim in the plan was false and only surfaced during code review (ob-9e9053d9).

payload.use_when: implementing or debugging a multi-source ETL command that runs several sub-sources and aggregates their results into a single process exit
payload.content: Report per-source exit status separately and exit non-zero only when the explicitly targeted source fails. Never collapse all sub-source failures into a single aggregate exit code; provide `--only <source>` for callers that need a clean signal for one source.
payload.causal_note: A single 404 from an unrelated github sub-source caused `autoetl run --full` to exit 1 even though the in-scope sessions transform had successfully processed 809 sessions, making it impossible to distinguish a target-source failure from an unrelated sub-source error (ob-56802d3a).

payload.use_when: writing a Go factory function that creates a derived event by delegating to a base constructor such as NewEvent()
payload.content: After calling NewEvent() inside a derived-event factory, immediately re-apply every identity/provenance field (Host, Source, Subject, CorrelationID, etc.) from the source event — NewEvent() auto-stamps those fields with the local machine's current context and will silently overwrite origin identity if you do not override them.
payload.causal_note: Prevents silent provenance corruption where derived events appear to originate from the forwarding host rather than the originating source, making distributed event traces incorrect and undebuggable without a test that asserts the forwarded field values.

payload.use_when: a Go module in the monorepo needs to consume types or functions defined in another module's internal/ packages
payload.content: Add thin pkg/ wrapper packages in the exporting module (type aliases plus delegating functions) rather than promoting internal/ paths or moving types into a shared module — this preserves the internal/ visibility contract, requires zero changes to the exporting module's existing call sites, and composes cleanly with go.work replace directives.

payload.use_when: adding a column to the ETL or search parquet schema and running integration tests against committed fixtures
payload.content: Regenerate all committed static parquet fixtures in the same PR or phase as any schema change that adds columns. Stale fixtures cause integration tests to fail with silent empty-value mismatches rather than actionable schema errors, making the root cause hard to diagnose.
payload.causal_note: auto-search/testdata/etl-output fixtures predated new columns added in a schema change; integration tests failed returning empty values with no schema error, not a clear missing-column message (ob-0556d782). Fixture regeneration was treated as a follow-up step rather than part of the schema-change phase.

payload.use_when: writing scanner tests, AST-pattern matcher tests, or golden-file tests for any language parser in auto-graph
payload.content: Include at least one test fixture per common syntactic variant (e.g. single-quoted and double-quoted imports in TypeScript); generate golden files end-to-end through the same binary path a user invokes — never from intermediate internal representations — so that normalization passes and canonicalization are exercised before the golden is written.
payload.causal_note: Double-quote-only fixtures allow single-quote sensitivity bugs to ship undetected; goldens generated from pre-canonicalization internal representations pass while asserting stale internal values instead of the public API contract.

payload.use_when: adding any warning, unresolved-import notice, or configuration diagnostic to a CLI command that outputs JSON in auto-graph or any auto-* package
payload.content: Write all diagnostics (unresolved imports, configuration warnings, scan errors) to stderr with structured fields (file, line, raw value, remediation hint); never add warning or diagnostic fields to the JSON output schema.
payload.causal_note: Adding a warning field to the JSON graph schema couples process-level diagnostics to the data contract, breaks downstream parsers, and violates the project-wide rule that stdout is a strictly parseable payload.

payload.use_when: implementing or enabling by default a CLI feature in any auto-* package that shells out to git (git ls-files, git rev-parse, git log) for file discovery or metadata
payload.content: Treat any non-zero exit from a git subprocess as a soft failure: log a warning to stderr and return an empty result rather than propagating the error; never let an opt-in-by-default git-dependent feature error out on directories that are not git repositories.
payload.causal_note: A scanner that shells out to git ls-files and propagates non-zero exits breaks all non-git project directories silently, regressing existing behavior for any project that did not previously use git.

payload.use_when: writing Go tests that require network access, external binary cloning, or other slow/online operations
payload.content: Gate every network-dependent or long-running Go test behind a `//go:build e2e` build tag so that `go test ./...` stays offline-safe and fast by default; document the explicit `-tags=e2e` invocation in the package CLAUDE.md and Makefile target.
payload.causal_note: Without the build tag, a single network-dependent test forces the default test run online, breaks CI in air-gapped environments, and slows every local test cycle — all silently, because the test appears to belong to the normal suite.

payload.use_when: reviewing a task plan where an acceptance criterion specifies `go test ./...` or equivalent automated validation
payload.content: When an AC requires `go test ./...` to validate a fixture or behaviour, reject any plan step that substitutes a manual smoke-check or binary invocation in its place; every such AC must map to an automated test case, and plan reviewers must flag the mismatch before implementation begins.
payload.causal_note: A manual run-and-inspect step looks like coverage during planning but leaves the AC unmet at CI time — the gap is invisible until a reviewer or the CI gate catches it after implementation is already done.
